SOUTH GATE CITY COUNCIL
  REGULAR MEETING AGENDA

  Monday, April 20, 2026 at 5:30 p.m.

  CONTINUED FROM APRIL 14, 2026 TO APRIL 20, 2026

  SOUTH GATE COUNCIL CHAMBERS
  8650 CALIFORNIA AVE
  SOUTH GATE, CA 90280

  VIEW MEETING LIVE ONLINE AT:
  HTTPS://WWW.YOUTUBE.COM/@SOUTHGATECA90280
City Officials
MAYOR, Joshua Barron  CITY CLERK, Yodit Glaze
VICE MAYOR, Al Rios  CITY TREASURER, Jose De La Paz
COUNCIL MEMBER, Maria del Pilar Avalos  CITY MANAGER, Rob Houston
COUNCIL MEMBER, Maria Davila  CITY ATTORNEY, Raúl F. Salinas
COUNCIL MEMBER, Gil Hurtado

If you would like to participate in this meeting, you can participate via the following
options:

1. VIEW THE MEETING LIVE ONLINE AT: South Gate, CA - YouTube
Please allow up to 24 hours after the meeting for the archive to be available.
2. PARTICIPATE BEFORE THE MEETING by emailing the City Clerk at:
yglaze@sogate.org no later than 4:00 p.m. on the day of the meeting. Please write
"Public Comment" in the subject line.
3. ATTEND THE MEETING IN PERSON
*The disruption in service of any alternative method does not prelude the City Council
or other legislative
body from taking further action and moving forward on the agenda.

  1
 Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,
closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

We envision a thriving, safe and inclusive community where everyone has the opportunity to access
exceptional services, education and support to be resilient and live full, vibrant lives.

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 4:00 pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be
summarized by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City
Council and will also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be
recorded for public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

Call to Order/Roll Call With Invocation & Pledge
CALL TO ORDER:  Joshua Barron, Mayor

INVOCATION:  Tina De La Rosa, Acting Director of Parks & Rec

PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE:  Jon F. Hamilton, Director of Human Resources

ROLL CALL:  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk

Presentations, Discussions, And Recommendations
  1. Budget Reduction: Community Development, Parks & Recreation,
  Administration/City Clerk and Action by Council

  The City Council will consider receiving and filing a presentation on Budget Reduction.
  (CD, PARKS, CM/CC and Action by Council)

  Documents:

  Item 1 Report 04142026.pdf

  2. Discussion Utility User Tax Measure to be Placed on the November 3, 2026 Ballot
  and Adding Budget Review Committee

  2
   The City Council will consider: (CM)

  a. Adopting a Resolution submitting ballot measure text for the Utility Users Tax Measure
  to the Voters at the November 3, 2026 General Municipal Election, request that the Los
  Angeles County Board of Supervisors (“Board of Supervisors”) authorize the Los Angeles
  County Registrar-Recorder / County Clerk (“County Elections Official”) to render all
  services necessary to conduct the Election, allow for Ballot Arguments, and an Impartial
  Analysis; and

  b. Reviewing the draft Ordinance for voter consideration of the Utility Users Tax.

  Documents:

  Item 2 Report 04142026.pdf

Public Hearings: None
Comments From The Audience - Non-Agenda Items
During this time, members of the public may address the City Council regarding any items not
listed on the agenda and within the subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council and not on
this agenda. Comments from the audience will be limited to three (3) minutes per speaker;
unless authorized by the Mayor, the time limit may not be extended by utilizing another
member's time. There will be no debate or action on items not listed on the agenda unless
authorized by law. The collective initial period of time for comments from the audience shall
be limited to 45 minutes. Any speaker that did not get a chance to speak during this segment
due to the 45-minute limitations will be able to speak at the end of the meeting prior to
adjournment.

Note: The City Council desires to provide all members of the public with the opportunity to
address the Council. Nevertheless, obscene language, comments intended to
disrupt/interfere, other actions which disrupt the progress of the meeting or slanderous
comments will not be tolerated and may result in ejection and/or may constitute a violation of
South Gate Municipal Code Section1.04.110.

Reports And Comments From City Officials
During this time, members of the City Council will report on matters pertaining to their service
on various intergovernmental boards and commissions as a representative of the City
pursuant to Assembly Bill 1234. City Council Members will also have an opportunity to
comment on matters not on the agenda.

Consent Calendar Items
Agenda Items 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11 are Consent Calendar Items. All items including
Ordinances, Resolutions and Contracts, may be approved by adoption of the Consent
Calendar, individually and collectively by one (1) motion. There will be no separate discussion
of these items unless Members of the City Council, the public, or staff request that specific

  3
 items be removed from the Consent Calendar for separate discussion and action. Members
of the public are permitted to speak on any item listed but their time period is limited to three
(3) minutes in total.

Any motion to introduce or adopt an Ordinance on the Consent Calendar shall be: (1) a
motion to waive the reading of the Ordinance and introduce the Ordinance or (2) a motion to
waive the reading of the Ordinance and adopt the Ordinance, as appropriate.

  3. Second Reading Adopting Ordinance No. 2026-02-CC for Park Curfew

  The City Council will consider: (CD)

  a. Find that this action is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
  pursuant to the General Rule Exemption under CEQA Guidelines Section 15061(b)(3), as
  there is no possibility that the ordinance amendment may have a significant effect on the
  environment, and as a Class 1 Categorical Exemption under CEQA Guidelines Section
  15301 (Existing Facilities), as the amendment involves only a minor change to the
  administrative hours of operation of existing park facilities with no physical alteration to
  the environment. The City Clerk is directed to file a Notice of Exemption with the County
  Clerk within five (5) working days of adoption.

  b. Waive further reading and adopt Ordinance No. 2026-02-CC amending Section
  7.49.150 of Chapter 7.49 of the South Gate Municipal Code relating to curfews in
  municipal parks.

  Documents:

  Item 3 Report 04142026.pdf

  4. Second Reading Adopting Ordinance No. 2026-03-CC for Electric Vehicle Charge
  Stations

  The City Council will consider: (CD)

  a. Find that the proposed addition to the South Gate Municipal Code adds provisions that
  are administrative in nature, do not approve any physical development, and do not have
  the potential to result in individually or cumulatively significant effects on the environment,
  and therefore, the passage of this ordinance is exempt from California Environmental
  Quality Act ("CEQA") review under the General Rule that CEQA only applies to projects
  with the potential to cause a significant effect on the environment and thus no
  environmental analysis or review is necessary- CEQA Guidelines Section 15061(b)(3).
  The City Clerk is directed to file a Notice of Exemption with the County Clerk within five
  (5) working days of adoption.

  b. Waive further reading and adopt Ordinance No. 2026-03-CC amending Title 9
  (Buildings) of the South Gate Municipal Code by the addition of new Chapter 9.14
  establishing a Streamlined Permitting Process for Electric Vehicle Charging Stations,
  consistent with California Government Code Section 65850.7 (AB 1236).

Deputy Director of Human Resources to serve as the second alternate Voting Director to

Contractors, Inc. for Construction of the Tweedy Mile Complete Streets Project,
#614-ST

a. Approving CCO No. 15 to Contract No. 2024-56-CC with Sequel Contractors, Inc., to
fund the accelerated construction schedule of 145 working days previously approved by
the City Council at the time of contract award of the Tweedy Mile Complete Streets
Project, City Project No. 614-ST, for an amount not to $350,000; and

b. Approving CCO No. 16 to Contract No. 2024-56-CC with Sequel Contractors, Inc., to

 reconcile final construction quantities, including bid item overruns and underruns, for the
Tweedy Mile Complete Streets Project, City Project No. 614-ST., in an amount not to

c. Appropriating $500,000 in Proposition C Funds to fund the cost of Contract Change

Tweedy Blvd. Complete Street Project Phase II, City Project No. 717-ST

The City Council will consider: (PW)

a. Approving the Memorandum of Understanding with the City of Lynwood for the Tweedy

b. Authorizing the Mayor to execute the MOU in a form acceptable to the City Attorney.

a. Receiving and Filing the Quarterly Investment Report for the quarter ended December
31, 2025

The City Council will consider: (CD)

a. Receiving and filing the General Plan and Housing Element APRs for calendar year
2025; and

b. Directing staff to file the APRs to HCD and OPR prior to the April 1, 2026, deadline.

Documents:

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, email, mail. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such
times when a State of Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current

  7
 meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

Recap  of Adopted  Budget
As reported  to the City  Council  on July  22, 2025,  the General  Fund  unassigned  balance  was
projected  to be $3,135,356  at June 30, 2026.  For fiscal  year 2025-26,  General  Fund revenues  are
budgeted  at $70,943,552  and expenditures  at $78,157,559,  resulting  in an ongoing  structural  gap
of $7,214,007.  Based  on current  projections,  this gap cannot  be addressed  solely  tmough  existing
recurring  revenues  without  service-level  adjustments  or the identification  of new revenue  sources.

This  structural  imbalance  reflects  the cumulative  impact  of several  long-term  fiscal  pressures.
These include  the expiration  of one-time  federal  relief  funding,  constraints  on property  tax growth
under  Proposition  13, volatility  in sales tax revenues,  declining  interest  earnings  as fund  balances
are drawn  down,  and significant  increases  in non-discretionary  costs such as pension  contributions,
insurance  premiums,  and  inflationary  impacts  on operations.  Collectively,  these  factors  have
resulted  in ongoing  expenditures  consistently  outpacing  recurring  revenues.

The FY 2025-26  structural  gap is currently  being  addressed  through  the use of one-time  solutions,
including  reserves  and interfund  transfers.  While  these measures  provide  short-term  budgetary
balance,  they do not resolve  the underlying  mismatch  between  ongoing  revenues  and expenditures
and are not sustainable  over the long term.

Based  on the City's  adopted  multi-year  financial  forecast,  the structural  deficit  is projected  to
exceed  $9,000,000  in FY 2026-27.  At that point,  available  discretionary  reserves  are expected  to
be largely  depleted,  limiting  the City's  ability  to continue  supporting  current  service  levels  without
corrective  action.

Absent  timely  action  to restore  structural  balance,  continued  reliance  on one-time  resources  will
reduce  financial  flexibility  and constrain  the City's  ability  to respond  to operational  needs  and
cornrnunity  priorities.  If  no  additional  recurring  revenue  is identified,  the  City  will  need  to
implement  approximately  $9.4 million  in ongoing  service  reductions  beginning  in FY  2026-27.
This  projected  growth  in the deficit,  from  $7.2  million  in FY  2025-26  to approximately  $9.4
million  in FY 2026-27,  reflects  the exhaustion  of most one-time  reserves  currently  used to bridge
the gap, combined  with  continued  escalation  in fixed  costs  such  as pension  contributions  and
insurance  premiums.

City's  Actions  to Close  the Budget  Deficit
The City  Council  and City  staff have taken proactive  steps to address the City's  growing  structural
imbalance,  recognizing  that early  action  is essential  to preserving  fiscal  stability  and maintaining
service  levels  for the community.  To be fiscally  responsible,  the City  has done the following:
  *  Reorganized  and consolidated  Departments  to create more  efficiency.
  *  Increased  fees for general  services,  and increased  sewer rates to eliminate  the general  fund
  from  subsidizing  that service.

  *  Reviewed  staff salary allocations  to maximize  the use of water and special  funding  sources.
  *  Reviewed  City  operations  for operational  and cost efficiencies.

City  staff and City  Council  continue  to review  operations  and reduce  City  costs; unfortunately,  the
scope  and  size  of the  General  Fund  deficit  caru'iot  be addressed  solely  through  cost-cutting
measures.

The City's structural General Fund deficit before expenditure  adjustments  was approximately  $9.4
million,  representing  the gap between  ongoing  revenues  and expenditures  absent corrective  action.
Through  $2.2 million  in expenditure  reductions  incorporated  into the FY 2025-26  adopted  budget,
this  gap has been  temporarily  partially  reduced  to $7.2 million  for  our  current  budget  year;
however,  the budget  continues  to reflect  an ongoing  structural  imbalance  that cannot  be resolved
through  one-time  measures  alone.

Addressing  this remaining  gap and restoring  long-term  structural  balance  will  require  additional
recurring  revenue,  further  service  reductions,  or a combination  of both.  Without  a stable  and
reliable  revenue  source,  the City  will  not be able to maintain  current  service  levels  over  time,
including  programs  such  as police  anti-gang  and  anti-drug  efforts,  neighborhood  graffiti
abatement,  after-school  and parks and recreation  programming,  and senior  services.

As proposed,  the City  Council  may  consider  placing  a Utility  Users  Tax measure  before  South
Gate voters.  If approved,  the revenue  generated  will  remain  locally  controlled,  meaning  the City
Council  retains  appropriation  authority  over how those :[unds are spent. Under  California  law, the
County  and State cannot  redirect  or reclaim  voter-approved  local tax revenues,  ensuring  that every
dollar  raised  would  stay in South  Gate to serve South  Gate residents.

Without  additional  recurring  revenue,  the City  will  be required  to implement  ongoing  reductions
to General  Fund  services  beginning  in the next  fiscal  year,  consistent  with  the magnitude  of the
remaining  structural  imbalance.  The City  remains  committed  to responsible  financial  stewardship
and will  continue  to pursue  every available  strategy,  including  expenditure  controls,  cost-recovery
improvements,  and economic  development,  to restore  structural  balance  and preserve  the services
our community  depends  on.

Required  Council  Actions
The City  Council  is being presented  with  all the required  resolutions  for action.  The resolution  that
approves  the ballot  question  with  a directive  for the City  Attorney  to prepare  an impartial  analysis
and provide  support  and opposition  arguments  and rebuttals  for the Election  ballot  requires  a two-
thirds  (2/3)  vote of all members  of the City  Council,  pursuant  to California  Government  Code  §
53724(b).  For South Gate's five-member  Council,  this means a minimum  of four affirmative  votes
is required  to place the measure  on the ballot.

The legal deadline  to place a ballot  measure  on the November  3, 2026,  election  ballot  is August  7,
2026.  A decision  now helps to ensure that all informational  materials  can be disseminated  to the

 voters  in a timely  fashion  and that there is ample  time  for the request  and collection  of absentee

Fiscal  Transparency
As part of the City's  commitment  to fiscal  transparency  and community  engagement,  Council  may
also  consider  establishing  a near-term  Ad  Hoc  Community  Finance  Committee  to provide  a
structured  public  perspective  on the City's  financial  condition  ahead of any ballot  measure.  The
Committee  would  convene  over approximately  three to four sessions during  the next five months,
with  a scope focused  on building  a foundational  understanding  of the City's  budget,  revenues,  and
expenditures;  reviewing  the  budget  reduction  and  revenue  enhancement  options  under
consideration;  and presenting  a summary  of findings  and observations  to the City  Council  in
September.  This  approach  would  provide  community-informed  context  for  the  Council's
deliberations  prior  to a potential  November  ballot  measure,  while  keeping  the Cornrnittee's  role
clearly  educational  and  advisory.  The  stnicture,  membership,  and process  guardrails  for  the
Cornrnittee  would  be developed  by  the  City  Manager's  Office  and presented  to  Council  for
consideration.

BACKGROUND:

The  City's  Current  Budget  Challenge
The City  is facing  a structural  budget  deficit,  meaning  the ongoing  cost of delivering  essential,
municipal  and utility  services  is higher  than the revenue  the City receives.  This deficit  is not a one-
time  issue;  it is ongoing  and long-term  and will  continue  to grow  unless  action  is taken.  Without
new,  reliable  funding,  the City  will  eventually  be unable  to maintain  current  service  levels.

Why  a Utility  Users  Tax  (UUT)?
A {JUT  would  provide  a stable,  dedicated  general  fund  revenue  source  to pay for City  services.
All  surrounding  south Los Angeles  cities  have an active  Utility  Users Tax to provide  significant
general  :[und revenue.  South Gate has never  had a Utility  Users Tax to fiind  general  fund services.

A UUT  would  provide  the stable,  recurring  revenue  needed  to close the City's  current  structural
gap and restore  its ability  to maintain  service  levels  without  continued  reliance  on one-time
reserves.  This funding  would  help close the structural  gap and ensure the City  can maintain  police,
parks and recreation,  community  development,  and public  works  services  for the cornrnunity.

Benefits  to Residents
A UUT  helps  the City  avoid  significant  service  reductions  in the future.  These  services  include
Police  911 response,  school  crossing  guards,  parks and recreation  facilities  and programs,  special
events,  planning,  building,  and code enforcement,  and public  works.  The UUT  also supports  long-
term financial  stability  and responsible  management  of community  resources.

The Cost  of Doing  Nothing
Without  a new revenue  source,  the City  will  need to consider:
  *  Cutting  service  levels,  including  municipal  and infrastructure  services.  The presentation
  outlines  the scope of the projected  budget  cuts to services  and the impacts  they will  have
  on the community.

   *  Delaying  maintenance  or upgrades,  which  can increase  long-term  costs.
  *  Using  emergency  reserves,  however,  the City's  discretionary  reserves,  primarily  the Budget
  Stabilization  Reserve,  are projected  to be substantially  drawn  down by the end of FY 2025 -
  26, with  the Emergency  Reserve  remaining  policy-protected.  Continued  reliance  on these
  limited  reserves  is neither  sustainable  nor fiscally  responsible  in the long term.

The UUT  is a proactive  measure  that  allows  the City  to stabilize  its budget,  protect  essential
services,  and plan responsibly  for the future.  The UUT  also provides  a fiinding  stream to preserve
vital  City  services.

 Section  7.29.120  Deficiency  Determination  and Assessment

  A.  The tax administrator  shall  make  a deficiency  determination  if he or she determines  that
  any person  required  to collect  or self-collect  taxes pursuant  to this chapter  has failed  to
  collect  and remit  the proper  amount  of tax,  including  but not limited  to, by improperly
  applying  or failing  to apply  the tax to one or more taxable  services  or charges.

  B.  The tax administrator  shall  mail  a notice  of such deficiency  determination  to the person
  required  to pay or remit  the tax, which  notice  shall refer briefly  to the amount  of the taxes
  owed,  plus interest  at the rate of three-quarters  of one (0.75)  percent  per month,  or any
  fraction  thereof,  on the tax due from  the date the city should  have received  the tax. Within
  14 calendar  days after service  of such notice,  the person  may make written  request  to the
  tax administrator  for a hearing.  If the person  fails to request  a hearing  within  that time,  the
  amount  of  the  deficiency  determination  shall  become  a final  assessment,  and  shall
  immediately  be due and owing  to the city.

  C.  If the person  requests  a hearing,  the tax administrator  shall cause the matter  to be set for
  hearing  not later than 30 days after receipt  of the request.  The tax administrator  shall mail
  notice  of the time  and place  of the hearing  to such person  at least 10 calendar  days before
  the hearing,  and the notice  may designate  records  that said person  must  produce  at such
  hearing.

  D.  At the time fixed  for the hearing,  the tax administrator  or his or her designee  shall hear all
  relevant  testimony  and evidence,  including  that  of any  other  interested  parties.  At  the
  discretion  of the tax administrator,  the hearing  may be continued  from time to time to allow
  presentation  of additional  evidence.  Within  a reasonable  time  following  the conclusion  of
  the hearing,  the tax administrator  or his or her designee  shall  issue a final  assessment
  confirming,  modifying,  or rejecting  the original  deficiency  determination,  and shall mail  a
  copy  of  such  final  assessment  to the person  owing  the tax.  The  decision  of  the  tax
  administrator  may  be appealed  pursuant  to Section  7.29.170  of this  chapter.  A hearing
  request  to the tax  administrator  and an appeal  to the city  council  pursuant  to  Section
  7.29. 170 of this chapter  are prerequisites  to a suit thereon.

  E.  Payment  of the  final  assessment  shall  become  delinquent  if  not  received  by  the  tax
  administrator  on or before  the 30th day following  service  of the notice  of final  assessment.
  The penalty  for delinquency  shall be 15% on the assessment,  along with  interest  at the rate
  of three-quarters  of one (0.75)  percent  per month,  or any fraction  thereof,  on the amount  of
  the tax, exclusive  of penalties,  from  the date of delinquency,  until  paid.

  b.  Waive  further  reading  and adopt  Ordinance  No.  2026-02-CC  amending  Section  7.49.150  of

FISCAL  IMPACT:  The proposed  ordinance  amendment  has no direct  fiscal  impact  to the City's

only.  The ordinance  does not appropriate  funds  or create new City  expenditures.

BACKGROUND:  SouthGateMunicipalCodeSection7.49.150currentlyestablishestwocategories
of park curfew:
  *  Parks with  buildings  or structures  available  for public  use: It is unlawful  for any person
  to remain,  stay, or loiter  in such municipal  parks  between  10:00  p.m.  and 5:00 a.m.,

   *  Parks  with  no buildings  or structures  available  for public  use: It is unlawful  for  any

Street  Soccer  USA

Street  Soccer  USA  is a nationally  recognized  nonprofit  organization  whose  mission  is to use
soccer  as a vehicle  for  positive  youth  development,  social  inclusion,  and  cornrnunity
empowerment.  The  organization  plans  to  begin  to  provide  structured  youth  soccer
programming  at Hollydale  Regional  Park beginning  Spring  2026.

Hollydale  Regional  Park,  located  within  the City,  is one of the City's  larger  recreational
facilities.  It currently  falls  within  the category  of parks  subject  to the sunset  curfew  under
Section  7.49.150(B).  Street  Soccer  USA's  programming-including  practices,  leagues,  and
events-is  anticipated  to run into evening  hours  that extend  beyond  sunset during  spring  and
fall months,  making  the current  curfew  framework  a practical  barrier  to program  delivery.

To accommodate  Street Soccer USA's  programming  and similar  future  needs, the City  initiated
a review  of Section  7.49.150  to evaluate  whether  a more  administratively  flexible  framework
could  be established.

ANALYSIS:

Proposed  Amendments  to Section  7.49.150

The proposed  ordinance  amends  Section  7.49.l50  to modify  Section  7.49.150(B)  to allow  permitted
or sponsored  city  activities  beyond  sunset  and to add two  new  subsections-Section  7.49.150(C)
(Extended  Park Hours)  and Section  7.49.150(D)  (Park  Closure)-while  retaining  the existing  curfew
framework  in Sections  7.49.150(A).

Section  7.49.150(C)  -  Extended  Park  Hours

The  proposed  new  subsection  (C)  delegates  authority  to the City  Manager,  or a duly  authorized
representative,  to extend  park  hours  of operation  beyond  the standard  curfew  hours  established  in
subsections  (A) and (B), subject  to the following  parameters  and safeguards:

*  No  extension  shall  result  in park  access  beyond  10 p.m.  without  prior  City  Council  approval,
  preserving  the City  Council's  legislative  authority  over significant  hour changes.

 @  The City Manager shall provide written notification to the City Council within five (5) business
  days of implementing any extended hours, ensuring transparency and Council awareness.
*  Any extension must be consistent with the purposes of Chapter 7.49 and serve the public health,
  safety, or general welfare.

The proposed subsection (C) satisfies these requirements by establishing clear outer limits (no access
beyond midnight without Council approval), a notification requirement, and a public welfare standard.

The practical effect of subsection (C) is to allow the City Manager to authorize extended hours at
specific parks-to  accommodate programtning and similar permitted activities, without the delay and
administrative burden of returning to the City Council for an ordinance amendment each time an
adjustment  is needed.

Section  7.49.150(D)  -  Park  Closure
The proposed new subsection (D) codifies the City Manager's authority to close a park area or
recreation facility at any time there is an apparent danger to persons using the property or for any cause
providing for the safety and protection of the public. This provision provides the City with a necessary
operational tool to respond to emergencies, hazardous conditions, or public safety concerns in atimely
manner. It is a natural complement to the extended hours authority in subsection (C), providing  a
symmetric framework for both expanding and restricting access based on conditions and needs.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  it is recommended  that the City  Council:

  the  South  Gate  Municipal  Code  by  the  addition  of  new  Chapter  9.14  establishing  a
  Streamlined  Permitting  Process  for  Electric  Vehicle  Charging  Stations,  consistent  with
  California  Government  Code Section  65850.7  (AB  1236).

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  The proposed  ordinance  would  streamline  the review  of electric  vehicle  charging
  stations  by eliminating  the current  Planning  Division  review  process  established  before  Building
  Division  permit  application  review.  The proposed  ordinance  will  result  in a reduction  of $563  in
  Architectural  Review  fees collected  for each electric  vehicle  charging  station  proposal  for the existing
  Planning  Division  review  process.

  BACKGROUND:  In 2015,  the California  Legislature  enacted  Assembly  Bill  1236  (Goverent
  Code Section  65850.7),  which  declared  the streamlined  permitting  of electric  vehicle  charging  stations
  (EVCS)  a matter  of statewide  concern  and imposed  a mandatory  obligation  by 2017 on all California

  1

  78
 cities  and counties  to adopt  an expedited,  streamlined  permitting  ordinance.  The Legislature's  intent
underlying  AB  1236 is to promote  electric  vehicle  adoption,  reducing  greenhouse  gas emissions,  and
removing  local  regulatory  barriers  that impede  the timely  and cost-effective  installation  of charging
infrastructure.  The City  did not satisfy  the State mandated  deadline  for the EVCS  ordinance  adoption
due to staffing  changes  and shortages  experience  in the Community  Development  Department  since
Assembly  Bill  1236 of the ordinance  is 2015.

AB 1236  establishes  the following  core requirements  applicable  to all local  agencies:

  *  All  EVCS  permit  applications  must  be approved  administratively  and  ministerially  by  the
  Building  Official  without  discretionary  planning  review  as long  as the  application  meets
  applicable  health  and safety  requirements.
  *  Local  review  is strictly  limited  to health  and safely  considerations.  Aesthetic,  design,  and land
  use review  are not permitted  grounds  for denial  or conditioning  of a EVCS  permit.
  *  Denial  is only  permitted  where  the Building  Official  makes  a written  finding,  supported  by
  substantial  evidence  that the installation  would  cause a specific,  adverse  impact  on public  health
  or safety that cannot  be feasibly  mitigated.
  *  Cities  must adopt a permitting  checklist  and make it available  online,  substantially  conforming  to
  the  State's  "Plug-In  Electric  Vehicle  Infrastructure  Permitting  Checklist"  published  by  the
  Governor's  Office  of Planning  and Research.
  *  Electronic  permit  submittal  and electronic  signatures  must be accepted.

The California  Legislature  further  strengthened  the AB  1236  mandate  in 2021  with  the enactment  of
Assembly  Bill  970 (Government  Code  Section  65850.71).  AB  970 added timelines  to the EVCS  permit
review  process  that includes:

  *  For  projects  of 1-25  charging  stations  at a single  site,  the Building  Official  must  deem  the
  application  complete  within  5 business  days  and approve  or deny  the application  within  20
  business  days of a complete  application.
  *  Forprojectsof26ormorechargingstationsatasinglesite,thecompletenessdeterminationmust
  occur  within  10 business  days  and approval  or denial  within  40 business  days  of a complete
  application.
  *  If the jurisdiction  fails to act within  these timeframes,  the application  is deemed  complete  and/or
  approved  by operation  of law.
  *  Only  one complete  set of written  deficiency  comments  may be issued.  The jurisdiction  may not
  introduce  new deficiencies  in subsequent  rounds  of review.

AB  1236  required  all cities  and counties  with  a population  of less than  200,000  residents  to adopt  a
compliant  EVCS  streamlining  ordinance  by  September  30, 2017.  Prompt  adoption  of the proposed
ordinance  is therefore  strongly  recommended  to bring  the City  into compliance  with  state law.

ANALYSIS:

The proposed  Ordinance  adds new  Chapter  9.14  (Streamlined  Permitting  Process  for Electric  Vehicle
Charging  Stations)  to Title  9 (Buildings)  of the South Gate Municipal  Code to establish  a clear, consistent
permitting  pathway  for all qualifying  EVCS  installations  within  the City.  The Chapter  applies  to the full
range  of charging  station  types  and installation  contexts  -  including  Level  1, Level  2, and DC Fast

  79
 Charging;  public  and private  stations;  residential  and cornrnercial  properties;  and both new installations
and modifications  to existing systems.  Upon  adoption  of the Ordinance,  the City's process  for EVCS
pernnit applications  would be as follows:

  *  Applicant  Self-Certification.  Before  submitting  a permit  application,  the applicant  verifies  that
  the proposed  installation  will  not have a specific,  adverse  impact  to public  health,  safety,  or
  building  occupants.  This pre-application  check covers electrical  system capacity  and loads, wiring
  and overcurrent protection,  building  infrastructure,  and the charging  station equipment  footprint
  and vehicle parking areas.
  *  Checklist-Based  Electronic  Submittal.  The  applicant  submits  a  permit  application
  electronically  via  approved  electronic  process  using  the City's  published  EVCS  permitting
  checklist. Electronic signatures are accepted in lieu of wet signatures.  The checklist  is required  to
  be posted on the City's website.
  *  Building  Division  Priority  Review  Upon  receipt,  the Building  Division  gives the application
  priority  review.  For projects  of 1 to 25 stations  at a single site, the Building  Official  must issue
  either a completeness  determination  or a written  deficiency  notice  within  5 business  days. For
  projects  of 26 or more stations, the Building  Official  has 10 business days. If the Building  Official
  fails to act within  these periods,  the application  is deemed complete  by operation  of state law.
  *  Single  Round  of Deficiency  Comments.  If the application  is incomplete,  the Building  Official
  issues one written deficiency notice identifying all deficiencies. Only one round of comments  is
  permitted. The City may not raise new deficiencies in later rounds of review.
  @  Health  and  Safety  Review  Only.  Once the application  is deemed  complete,  the Building
  Official's  review  is strictly  limited  to whether  the proposed  EVCS  meets applicable  health and
  safety requirements of local, state, and federal law. Review  of aesthetic, design, or land use factors
  is not permitted under state law.
  *  Mandatory  Timelines.  For projects  of 1 to 25 stations,  the Building  Official  must approve  or
  deny the complete  application  within  20 business days. For projects  of 26 or more stations,  the
  deadline is 40 business days. If the City fails to act within  these timeframes,  the permit  is deemed
  approved by operation of state law.
  *  Permit  Issuance.  Upon  confirming  that the application  is complete  and meets all applicable
  requirements,  the Building  Official  administratively  approves  the application  and issues  all
  necessary  building  permits  and authorizations.  No planning  permit,  discretionary  approval,  or
  conditional  use permit may be required  unless the Building  Official  makes a written  finding  based
  on substantial evidence that the installation  would  cause a specific,  adverse  impact  on public
  health or safety that cannot be mitigated.

  CONCLUSION:

  The adoption  of the EVCS  streamlining  ordinance  by addition  of Chapter  9.14 to the South Gate
  Municipal  Code is a necessary  and overdue  action  that will  bring  the City into compliance  with the

  requirements  of State Law by establishing  a ministerial,  by-right  approval  process for quali:tying  EVCS

  Providing  a clear, fast, and reliable  permitting  pathway  supports the community  need, reduces costs for

9.14.010-  Purpose.

The purpose  of this Chapter  is to promote  and encourage  the use of electric  vehicles  by creating  an
expedited,  streamlined  permitting  process  for  electric  vehicle  charging  stations  while  promoting
public  health  and safety  and preventing  specific  adverse impacts  in the installation  and use of such
charging  stations.  The provisions  of this  Chapter  have been prepared  to comply  with  California
Government  Code Section  65850.7.

9.14.020-  Definitions.

  A.  "Electric  vehicle  charging  station"  or "charging  station"  means  any level  of electric
vehicle  supply  equipment  station  that is designed  and built-in  compliance  with  Article  625 of the
California  Electrical  Code, as it reads on the effective  date of this Chapter,  and delivers  electricity  from
a source outside an electric  vehicle  into a plug-in  electric vehicle.

  B.  "Specific,  adverse  impact"  means a significant,  quantifiable,  direct,  and unavoidable
impact,  based on objective,  identified,  and written  public  health  or safety  standatds,  policies,  or
conditions  as they existed on the date the application  was deemed complete.

  C.  "Electronic  submittal"  means the utilization  of one or more of the following:

  1.  Electronic  mail or email.

  2.  The internet.

  3.  Any  other electronic  submittal  process  as approved  by the Building  Official.

  D.  "Building  Official"  means  the Building  Official  for the City  of South  Gate and/or
the Building  Official's  designee.

 9.14.030-  Expedited  permitting  process.

Consistent  with  Government  Code  Section  65850.7,  the  Building  Official  shall  implement  an
expedited,  streamlined  permitting  process for electtaic vehicle  charging  stations,  and adopt a checklist
of all requirements  with  which  electric  vehicle  charging  stations  shall comply  with  to be eligible  for
expedited  review.  The  expedited,  streamlined  permitting  process  and checklist  may  refer  to the
recommendations  contained  in the most current  version  ofthe  "Plug-In  Electric  Vehicle  Infrastnicture
Permitting  Checklist"  of  the  "Zero-Emission  Vehicles  in  California:  Community  Readiness
Guidebook"  as published  by the Governor's  Office  of Planning  and Research.  The City's  adopted
checklist  shall be published  on the City's website.

9.14.040-  Electric  vehicle  charging  station  installation  requirements.

  A.  Electric  vehicle  charging  station  equipment  shall  meet  the requirements  of the
California  Electrical  Code,  the  Society  of  Automotive  Engineers,  the  National  Electrical
Manufacturers  Association,  and accredited  testing  laboratories  such as Underwriters  Laboratories,
and rules  of the Public  Utilities  Commission  or a Municipal  Electric  Utility  Company  regarding
safety  and reliability.

  B.  Installation  of  electric  vehicle  charging  stations  and  associated  wiring,  bonding,
disconnectu'ig  means and overcurrent  protective  devices shall meetthe  requirements  of Article  625 and
all applicable  provisions  of the California  Electrical  Code.

  C.  Installation  of electric  vehicle  charging  stations  shall be incorporated  into the load
calculations  of all  new  or existing  electrical  services  and  shall  meet  the requirements  of the
California  Electrical  Code.  Electric  vehicle  charging  equipment  shall be considered  a continuous
load.

  D.  Anchorage  of  either  floor-mounted  or wall-mounted  electric  vehicle  charging
stations  shall meet the requirements  of the California  Building  or Residential  Code as applicable
per occupancy,  and the provisions  of the manufacturer's  installation  instructions.  Mounting  of
charging  stations  shall not adversely  affect  building  elements.

9.14.050-  Permit  application  process.

  A.  Prior  to submitting  an application  for processing,  an applicant  shall verify  that the
installation  of an electric  vehicle  charging  station  will  not have specific,  adverse  impact  to public
health and safety and building  occupants.  Verification  by the applicant  includes  but is not limited  to:
electrical  system  capacity  and loads;  electrical  system  wiring,  bonding  and overcurrent  protection;
building  infrastructure  affected  by charging  station  equipment  and associated  conduits;  areas of
charging  station  equipment  and vehicle  parking.

application  for  an electric  vehicle  charging  station  that  meets  the  requirements  of the  City's
checklist.  A permit  application  that  satisfies  the information  requirements  in the City's  adopted
checklist,  as determined  by the Building  Official,  shall process  as follows:

 BACKGROUND:  The City of South Gate ("City")  is a member  of ICRMA,  a joint  powers  authority
 created  pursuant  to the provisions  of the Joint  Powers  Act  under  Section  6500  of the California
 Government  Code.  ICRMA  provides  a Liability  Program,  Workers'  Compensation  Program,  Property
 Program,  and other coverage  programs  for its members.  The Joint Powers  Agreement  provides  that
 each member  agency is required  to appoint  one Voting  Director  to the Board and may appoint  no more
 than two alternates  in order to ensure attendance  and representation  at ICRMA  Board meetings.  The
 City  Council  of each member  city  may  select  and change  any of its representatives  by filing  a
 Resolution  with  ICRMA.  The City  Council  may  appoint  elected member(s)  or staff member(s)  to
 serve  on  the Governing  Board.  Staff members  shall include  the City Manager,  a staff member  holding
 a position  with  the authority  equivalent  to a Department  Director,  or a staff member  dedicated  (full-
 time) to risk management.  In making  such an appointment,  the City Council  may appoint  a specifically
 named individual  or a specific  position,  such as Director  of Human  Resources  or Deputy  Director  of
 Human  Resources.

  91
 On August  8, 2023,  at the regularly  scheduled  City  Council  Meeting,  the City  Council  approved  a
Resolution  affirming  the appointments  of City  Council  Member  Maria  Davila  to serve as the City's
Voting  Director  to the ICRMA  Board,  the Director  of Human  Resources  to serve as the first  alternate
Voting  Director  on the ICRMA  Board  in the absence  of the primary  Voting  Director,  and the Risk
Manager  to serve as the second  alternate  Voting  Director  on the ICRMA  Board  in the absence  of the
primary  Voting  Director  and the first  alternate  Voting  Director.

Due to the required  reduction  in the Human  Resources  budget  and the elimination  of the Risk Manager
position,  who  regularly  attended  all ICRMA  Board  meetings,  the duties  of the Risk  Manager  will  be
transferred  to Human  Resources  Department  staff  as part  of its required  reorganization.  The  City's
current  Deputy  Director  of Human  Resources  previously  served  as a Voting  Director  on the ICRMA
Board  and, therefore,  will  resume  this risk  management  function  as a result  of the elimination  of the
Risk  Manager  position.  While  the Deputy  Director  of Human  Resources  performs  duties  related  to the
'Jull-time  function  of risk management,  the position  also has the authority  of the Department  Director  in
his/her  absence.

Accordingly,  staff  requests  that  the  City  Council  adopt  a Resolution  reappointing  City  Council
Member  Maria  Davila  as the City's  Voting  Director  to the ICRMA  Board,  appoint  the position  of
Director  of Human  Resources  as the first  alternate  Voting  Director  to the ICRMA  Board,  and the
position  of Deputy  Director  of  Human  Resources  as the  second  alternate  Voting  Director  to the
ICRMA  Board.  The effective  date of these  appointments  shall  be May  1, 2026.  This  revised  action
provides  flexibility  to the City  to continue  to send appropriate  Voting  Directors  to the ICRMA  Board
meeting  without  the City  Council  having  to adopt  a new  Resolution  each time  there  is a change  in
personnel.

SUBJECT:  LICENSE  AGREEMENT  WITH  THE  LOS  ANGELES  DEPARTMENT  OF
WATER  AND  POWER  FOR  THE  I-710  FIRESTONE  BOULEVARD  SOUTHBOUND  ON
RAMP  MODIFICATION  PROJECT,  CITY  PROJECT  N0.  354-ST

PURPOSE:  To approve  a License  Agreement  with  the Los Angeles  Department  of Water  and Power
("LADWP")  necessary  for  the construction  of the I-710  Firestone  Boulevard  Southbound  On Ramp
Modification  project,

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Approving  a License  Agreement  with  LADWP  to obtain  authorization  to construct  sidewalk
  improvements  as a part of the I-710  Firestone  Boulevard  Southbound  On Ramp  Modification,
  City  Project  No.  354-ST,  and provide  compensation  to LADWP  in the amount  of $28,590  for
  the two-year  term agreement;  and
  b.  Authorize  the Mayor  to execute  the Agreement  in a form  acceptable  to the City  Attorney.

FISCAL  IMPACT:  There  is no impact  to the General  Fund.  The $28,590  License  Agreement  will
be funded  with  Measure  R Metro  Grant  Funds  budgeted  in the FY  2026/27  CIP.  The two-year  cost
includes  $5,082  (Year  1), $5,336  (Year  2), and an $18,172  security  deposit.

ANALYSIS:  The  Project  includes  construction  of  a new  sidewalk,  ADA  ramps,  and  crosswalk
improvements  along  Firestone  Boulevard  at the  southbound  I-710  on-ramp.  To  complete  these
improvements,  the  City  requires  approximately  92 square  feet  of LADWP-owned  property  located
along  the  southerly  side  of  Firestone  Boulevard  over  the  Los  Angeles  River  to  coru'iect  the  new
sidewalk  to the existing  bridge  sidewalk.

The  City  has coordinated  with  LADWP  over  the past  two  years  to secure  access  to the required
property,  In March  2026,  LADWP  provided  a License  Agreement  authorizing  the  City  to enter  its
property  and construct  the proposed  improvements.  Approval  of the Agreement  is needed  to proceed
with  construction.

The Agreement  has a two-year  term  at a total  cost of $28,590,  including  $5,082  for Year 1, $5,336  for
Year 2, and an $18,172  security  deposit.  Upon  execution,  LADWP  is expected  to pursue  a long-term
agreement,  anticipated  to be a 30-year  term,  for continued  use of the improvements.

  95
 BACKGROUND:  The  I-710  Firestone  Boulevard  Southbound  On-Ramp  Modification  Project  is
included  in the Fiscal  Year  2026/27 Capital  Improvement  Program  with  a budget  of $16.829  million.
The project  is intended  to improve  safety  and reduce  congestion  along the corridor.

The  primary  improvement  involves  realigning  and  widening  the  southbound  ramp  to  match  the
recently  widened  roadway.  Additional  work  includes  installation  of ADA-compliant  ramps,  concrete
barriers,  a new ramp metering  signal,  shoulder  lanes, and guardrails;  removal  of existing  pavement  and
construction  of new pavement  and concrete  base; upgrades  to the drainage  system;  new  signing  and
striping,  including  merging  signs;  and  installation  of irrigation  and  landscaping,  along  with  other
related  improvements.

Design  of the Project  is in its final  stages.  The next  step is to obtain  authorization  from  Caltrans  to
proceed  with  construction.  The design  plans were approved  by Caltrans  on September  18, 2024.  Upon
approval  of the License  Agreement,  Caltrans  will  be able to certify  the required  right-of-way  and issue
the Authorization  to Proceed  with  Construction  (E-76),  allowing  the Project  to move  forward  to bid
and construction.

The total  project  budget  is $16.83M.  It is funded  with  $8.2M  in Metro  Fund,  $8.63M  of Demo  TEA
21 Funds  and $55K  in Proposition  C Funds.

It is estimated  that construction  will  begin  in late 2026 and be completed  in about 16 months.

300.  Maintenance

  300.1  Maintenance  and  Repair

  Licensee  shall  be responsible  for the maintenance  of Licensed  Area
  and shall  keep  the area  in a neat  and clean  condition  within  the
  LADWP  Transmission  Line  Rights-of-Way  (TLRW).  Licensee  will
  assume  responsibility  for the maintenance  of the project
  improvements,  and for all the risks  and  liabilities  associated  with the
  construction  and installation  of Licensee's  facilities  in accordance  with
  terms  and conditions  of this License  Agreements  and  ,
  Standard  Conditions  for Construction.  LADWP  will not be liable  for any
  damage  to the facilities  during  LADWP's  operation  and maintenance
  activities.  Licensee  must  obtain  any and all permits  and environmental
  clearances  required  for such  maintenance  and repair.

301.  Transmission  Line  Right-of-Way

  301 .1  High-Voltage  Electric  Lines

  The  LADWP  TLRW  contains  high-voltage  electric  lines;  therefore,
  Licensee  shall  utilize  only such  equipment,  material,  and construction
  techniques  that are permitted  under  applicable  safety  ordinances,  and
  statutes,  including  the following:  California  Code  of Regulations,  Title
  8, Industrial  Relations  Chapter  4, Division  of Industrial  Safety,
  Subchapter  5. Electrical  Safety  Orders,  California  Public  Utilities
  Commission,  General  Order  No. 95, Rules  for Overhead  Electric  Line
  Construction  and  General  Order  No. 128,  Rules  for Construction  of
  Underground  Lines.

  301.2  Equipment  Under  LADWP  TLRW

  No equipment  shall  be allowed  to setup  directly  below  the LADWP
  TLRW,  without  the written  approval  of LADWP  and in accordance  with
  , Standard  Conditions  for Construction.  Licensee  shall  provide
  LADWP's  Transmission  Construction  and  Business  Group  a list of all
  equipment  to be used  for construction  operations  at least  fourteen  (14)
  calendar  days  prior  the start  of construction.  Contact  LADWP's
  Transmission  Construction  and Business  Group  at (818)  771-5031  or
  (818)  771-5076.

302.  Operations

  302.1  Hazardous  Activity

  If LADWP  determines  at any time  that Licensee's  activities  are
  hazardous  or detrimental  to the LADWP  TLRW,  LADWP  shall  have  the
  right  to immediately  terminate  said  activities,  and,  if necessary,  to
  terminate  the License  Agreement.

  302.2  Acknowledgement

  Licensee  shall  acknowledge  that the LADWP  TLRW  are integral
  components  of the transmission  line system,  which  provides  electric
  power  to the City of Los Angeles  and other  local  communities.  Their
  use is under  the jurisdiction  of the North  American  Electric  Reliability
  Corporation  (NERC),  an organization  of the Federal  Energy  Regulatory
  Commission  (FERC).  Safety  and protection  of critical  facilities  are the
  primary  factors  used  to evaluate  secondary  land  use proposals.  The
  LADWP  TLRW  serves  as a platform  for access,  construction,  facility
  expansion  and emergency  operations.  Therefore,  the proposed  use
  may,  from  time  to time,  be subject  to temporary  disruption  caused  by
  such  operations.

 ANALYSIS:  Construction  of the Tweedy  Mile  Complete  Streets  Project  is completed,  and final
construction  costs have been reconciled.  Two  change  orders  are needed  to fully  fund  construction
costs.  A summary  of the change  orders  is listed  below:

  *  CCONo.l5:Atthetimeofcontractaward,theCityCouncilapproveda$350,000incentive
  to complete  constniction  on an accelerated  schedule  of 145 working  days. The incentive  was
  included  in the contractor's  bid. The contractor  met this obligation  thus payment  is now  due.
  CCO No. 15 will  authorize  payment.

  *  CCO  No.  16: Reflects  final  payment  adjustments  based  on the actual  quantities  of work
  constructed  compared  to the original  bid item  estimates.  As is typical  in construction,  some
  bid items  resulted  in over-runs  where  field  conditions  required  more  work  than anticipated,
  while  others  resulted  in under-runs  where  less work  was needed.  The  net effect  of these
  quantity  adjustments  across  all bid items  results  in a total  increase  not to exceed  $144,793
  for the project.

The  total  in  change-order  costs  is $494,793,  which  will  be funded  by  the  proposed  $500,000
Proposition  C appropriation.  The balance  will  be used to cover staff time  and project-related  costs.

BACKGRO{JND:  Construction  of the Tweedy  Mile  Complete  Streets Project  has been completed.
The project  delivered  safely,  traffic  circulation,  landscaping,  and beautification  improvements  along
Tweedy  Boulevard  from  Dearborn  Avenue  to Dorothy  Avenue.

The  improvements  enhance  pedestrian  and  traffic  safety,  improve  access  to public  transit  and
bicycle  facilities,  address  deferred  maintenance,  and provide  overall  quality-of-life  benefits  to the
corridor.  Work  included  pavement  rehabilitation;  new  sidewalks  and ADA-compliant  curb  ramps;
enhanced  crosswalks,  including  four flashing  beacon  crossings;  traffic  calming  features  such as curb
extensions  and mid-block  bulbouts;  upgraded  signage;  replacement  of street  fiirniture  and bus stop
amenities;  new landscaping;  installation  of sharrows;  and new bicycle  racks.

On July 9, 2024, the City  Council  awarded  Contract  No. 2024-56-CC  to Sequel  Contractors  Inc., for
the construction  of the Project  in the amount  of $7,745,175.  The City  Council  also authorized  the
City  Manager  to approved  change  orders  administratively  up to an amount  of $800,000.

To date, a total  of 14 CCOs  to Contract  No.  2024-56-CC  were approved  administratively,  totaling
$666,651,  and fully  fiinded  with  budgeted  fiinds.  The CCOs  are summarized  below:

  @  CCO  No.  I was  approved  in the amount  of $1,362.  Work  included  the following:  The
  procurement  of 32 additional  pedestrian  signs in Spanish  for the use of the project.

  *  CCO No. 2 was approved  in the amount  of $120,511  to remove  and replace  all pavers  at the
  crosswalks  along  Tweedy  Boulevard  between  Dearborn  Avenue  and Dorothy  Avenue.

  *  CCO  No.  3 was approved  in the amount  of $7,705  to adjust  a catch  basin  on the north  side
  of Tweedy  Boulevard,  east of San Vicente  Avenue,  to match  the new sidewalk  grade.

  *  CCO No. 4 was approved  in the amount  of $20,000 to remove  a rusted  streetlight  at the
  northwest  corner  of San Gabriel  Avenue  and install  a new  foundation  for a City-furnished
  replacement.

   *  CCO  No.  5 was approved  in the amount  of $1,766  to install  drainage  grates  and pipes  to
  prevent  water  from  pooling  on the new sidewalks.

  *  CCO  No.  6 was approved  in the amount  of $1,931  to remove  an old foundation  discovered
  during  streetlight  relocation  at Tweedy  Boulevard  and Virginia  Avenue.

  *  CCO  No.  7 was approved  in the amount  of $88,425  to remove  unexpected  concrete  found
  beneath  the roadway  so new asphalt  could  be installed  at the required  thickness.

  *  CCO  No.  8 was approved  in the amount  of $117,507  to construct  five  concrete  bus pads in
  place of standard  asphalt  for improved  durability.

  *  CCO  No. 9 was approved  in the amount  of $84,074  to remove  existing  concrete  at bulbouts
  and parklets  to allow  construction  per plans.

  *  CCO No. 10 was approved  at no cost to complete  additional  paving  work  at select locations
  due to paver removal;  the contractor  was granted  four additional  working  days.

  @  CCO  No. 11 was approved  in the amount  of $2,376  to update  wayfinding  signs to include
  the City  logo and revised  colors.

  *  CCO  No.  12  was  approved  in the  amount  of  $97,476  to  add  striping,  including  high-
  visibility  crosswalks,  following  removal  of pavers.

  *  CCO  No.  13 was  approved  in the  amount  of  $32,274  to  install  artificial  vines,  replace
  damaged  trellis  panels,  and add landscaping  east of California  Avenue.

  *  CCO No. 14 was approved  in the amount  of $91,250  to install  three  City  logos  at California
  Avenue,  Otis Street,  and Alexander  Avenue.

Construction  of the Project  began on August  12, 2024,  and was completed  on May  30, 2025.

SUBJECT:  MEMORANDUM  OF UNDERST ANDING  WITH THE CITY OF LYNWOOD
FOR THE TWEEDY  BOULEVARD  COMPLETE  STREET  PROJECT  PHASE II, CITY
PROJECT  N0. 717-ST

PURPOSE:  To approve a Memorandum of Understanding ("MOU")  with the City of Lynwood
for the Tweedy Boulevard Complete Street Project Phase II ("Project") to facilitate construction of
improvements within Lynwood's jurisdiction and provide for reimbursement of project costs.

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City Council will consider:
  a.  Approving the Memorandum of Understanding with the City of Lynwood for the Tweedy
  Boulevard Complete Street Phase II, City Project No. 717-ST; and
  b.  Authorizing the Mayor to execute the MOU in a form acceptable to the City Attorney.

FISCAL IMPACT:  There is no impact to the General Fund. The proposed MOU authorizes the
City of South Gate to fund and construct improvements within the City of Lynwood, with full
reimbursement by the City of Lynwood for actual costs of design, construction, and construction
management, estimated at $447,846.

ANALYSIS:  The Project includes improvements along two segments: (l) Alameda Street to
Dearborn Avenue, and (2) Dorothy Avenue to the Los Angeles River Bicycle Trail. A portion of
Tweedy Boulevard within the project limits lies within the jurisdiction of the City of Lynwood,
specifically between 165 feet west of Long Beach Boulevard and 160 feet east of State Street. As
such, Lynwood's approval is required to construct improvements within its jurisdiction, as well as
to 'fund its share of the project costs.

Staff have coordinated with the City of Lynwood, which has expressed interest in participating in
the Project. This participation  will be formalized through a MOU, under which Lynwood will
authorize the improvements within its jurisdiction  and agree to reimburse the City of South Gate for
its proportionate share of project costs. Accordingly,  City Council approval and execution of the
proposed MOU is recommended.

It is noted that the City Council  of the City of Lynwood  approved the subject MOU  February 17,
2026.

  1

  363
 BACKGROUND:  The Project  is included  in the Capital  Improvement  Program  and will  enhance
pedestrian,  bicycle,  and  motorist  safety  while  addressing  deferred  maintenance  along  Tweedy
Boulevard.  Improvements  include  road  rehabilitation;  traffic  signal  modifications  at Long  Beach
Boulevard  and State  Street;  high-visibility  crosswalks;  ADA  ramps;  corner  bulb-outs;  pedestrian
rapid  flashing  beacons  at three intersections;  signing  and striping;  and installation  of street furniture,
including  bus shelters,  bike racks, trash receptacles,  landscaping,  and shade trees.

Staff coordinated  with  the City  of Lynwood  to prepare  a MOU  to authorize  improvements  within  its
jurisdiction  and provide  for reimbursement  of associated  project  costs.  Highlights  of the agreement
 include the following:

  *  TheAgreementshallbeeffectivefromAprill4,2026,throughDecember31,2027.

  *  The City  of Lynwood  shall be responsible  for 'funding  the portion  of project  costs within  its
  jurisdiction,  not covered  by grant fiinding.  It is estimated  that $873,438  in grant funds will
  be applied  toward  improvements  in Lynwood,  with  an estimated  remaining  balance  of
  $447,846  to be funded  by Lynwood.

  *  Improvements  within  Lynwood  are shown  in Attachment  "B"  and include  traffic  signal
  modifications,  signing  and striping,  ADA  ramps,  street :[urniture,  bus shelters,  concrete
  improvements,  and road rehabilitation.

  *  Lynwood  shall reimburse  the City  of South  Gate for actual  costs associated  with  design,
  construction,  and construction  management  for improvements  within  its jurisdiction.

The project's  design  phase is planned  for completion  in June 2026.  Construction  is plaru'ied  to begin
in late 2026 and be completed  within  9 months.

  SUBJECT:  INVESTMENT  REPORT  QUARTER  ENDING  DECEMBER  31, 2025

  PURPOSE:  California  Government  Code  Section  53646  requires  staff  to submit  a report  to the
  City  Council  and City  Manager,  at least  quarterly,  which  provides  detailed  information  on all
  investments  of the City.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  The City  Council  will  consider  receiving  and filing  the Quarterly
  Investment  Report  for the quarter  ended December  31, 2025.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  Interest  earnings  totaled  $821,583  for the quarter.

  ANALYSIS:  See Executive  Summary  and Background  and Analysis  sections  below.

  EXECUTIVE  SUMMARY:  As of December  31, 2025,  the City's  investment  portfolio  totaled
  $96,516,053 at cost and $96,454,157 at market  value.  The portfolio  generated  $821,583 in interest
  earnings  during  the quarter  and remains  fully  compliant  with  the City's  Investment  Policy  and
  California  Government  Code  Section  53600  et seq. All  investments  are structured  to preserve
  capital,  ensure  sufficient  liquidity  for operational  needs,  and deliver  a reasonable  rate of return
  within  those constraints.  There  are no compliance  issues,  credit  concerns,  or liquidity  constraints
  to  report.  The  portfolio  continues  to  perform  as intended,  providing  stable  earings  while
  maintaining  a highly  liquid  and low-risk  position  to support  City  operations.

  While  investment  earnings  provide  a meaningful  supplemental  revenue  source,  the portfolio  is
  managed  primarily  to ensure the safety  and availability  of public  'funds. It is not intended  to offset
  the City's  ongoing  structural  imbalance  between  revenues  and expenditures.

  BACKGROUND  AND  ANALYSIS:  California  Goven'unent  Code  Section  53646  requires
  quarterly  reports  to the City  Council  detailing  investment  activity  and portfolio  status.

  This report  provides  the City  Council  with  a current  snapshot  of the City's  investment  holdings,
  liquidity  position,  and compliance  with  applicable  laws and policies  as of December  31, 2025.

  382
 Attachments  include  detailed  investment  listings,  cash balances, and prior-quarter  reports for
reference.

Consistent with the City's broader financial reporting, this report reflects the City's position at a
point in time. It should be considered alongside the City's budget and multi-year financial outlook,
which address the sustainability of ongoing operations.

Attached are the Investment Reports for the quarter ending December 31, 2025, for the City and
Housing Authority  (Attachment A), including the corresponding Schedule of Cash Balances
(Attachment B). This submission provides the latest available valuation of the City's investment
portfolio and serves to apprise the Council of the City's financial position as of the end of the first
half of this fiscal year. Prior-quarter investment reports for September 30, June 30, and March 31,
2025, are included as Attachments C through E. Those reports were not previously presented to
the City Council due to administrative delays; they are provided here in the interest of transparency
and to give Council a complete view of portfolio activity over the fiscal year.

Portfolio  Overview
The  is invested in high-quality,
  portfolio  fixed-income instruments consistent with the City's
conservative investment policy. As of December 31, 2025, the portfolio was allocated as follows:
67.52% in the U.S. Bank First American Treasury Obligation money market fund ($65,168,467);
17.80% in the Local Agency Investment Fund ($17,183,950); 13.39% in U.S. Government and
Governrnent Agency Issues ($12,921,637);  and 1.29% in brokered certificates  of deposit
($1,242,000). All securities are held under U.S. Bank's safekeeping. Portfolio balances declined
from $106. 1 million as of December 31, 2024 to $96.5 million as of December 31, 2025, primarily
reflecting the drawdown of LAIF balances to support operational cash flow needs, with LAIF
decreasing from $29.3 million  to $17.2 million  over that period.

Liquidity  and Maturity  Profile
The  portfoliomaintains a highly liquid posture. The money market and LAIF positions, which
together  represented 85.32% of the portfolio ($82,352,417) at the close of December 2025, are
available on a next-day basis. As of December 31, 2025, there were no fixed-income  securities
with maturities  beyond one year; the furthest scheduled maturity was December 9, 2026, at 343
days. This structure ensures the City has ready access to funds to meet payroll, vendor obligations,
and all other operational  requirements without liquidity  constraints. The total citywide cash
balance  as of December 31, 2025, was $102,294,011,  of which $96,516,053 was invested, and
$5,777,957 was uninvested.

Investment  Performance
The City's investment portfolio earned $821,583 in interest during the quarter ended December
31, 2025. On an annualized basis, the portfolio generated an estimated yield of approximately
3.3%.

For  context,a comparable benchmark, the State's Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF),  was
earning approximately 4.2% to 4.5% during the same period. The difference is explained by 12
older bonds the City purchased in 2021, when interest rates were near historic lows. Those bonds
earn an average of only O.8% and are reducing the portfolio's overall return. The good news is that

  383
  7-
 all 12 bonds  mature  by November  2026,  after  which  those  funds  can be reinvested  at current,
higher  rates. Investment  earnings  are expected  to improve  as that happens.

The portfolio's  paper  value  relative  to its purchase  price  also improved  significantly  during  the
fiscal  year, from  a difference  of ($708,259) as of December  31, 2024, to ($61,897) as of December
31, 2025,  as those older bonds  approached  their  maturity  dates. All  investments  remain  compliant
with  the City's  Investment  Policy,  and overall  performance  meets  expectations  given  the City's
emphasis  on safety  and liquidity.

Policy  Compliance
All  investments  held during  the quarter  were made in full  compliance  with  the City's  Investment
Policy  and California  Governrnent  Code  Sections  53600  through  53607.  Permitted  investment
types  include  U.S.  government  and agency  securities,  LAIF,  money  market  funds,  and FDIC-
insured  certificates  of deposit,  all of which  are represented  in the current  portfolio.  Per policy,
maximum  maturity  is five  years;  the  current  portfolio's  longest  maturity  is 343  days.  No
exceptions,  violations,  or credit  events were identified  during  the quarter.  Staff certify  that the City
has sufficient  cash flow  from  investments  maturing  or from  liquid  funds  to meet all anticipated
expenditures  for the next six months.

Strategic  Outlook
Staff  will  continue  to monitor  interest  rate  conditions  and cash flow  needs  over  the coming
quarters.  The portfolio  will  remain  conservatively  positioned,  with  an emphasis  on maintaining
high  liquidity  while  capturing  available  short-term  yields.  As  interest  rates  evolve,  staff  will
evaluate  opportunities  to optimize  returns  within  the constraints  of the City's  Investment  Policy.

In March  2026, the City retained  Meeder  Public  Funds as its investment  manager  -  the City's  first
actively  managed  investment  relationship  in many  years.  Meeder  has begun  transitioning  the
portfolio  and  will  provide  ongoing  guidance  on  investment  strategy,  security  selection,  and
reinvestment  decisions  as the legacy  bonds mature  throughout  2026. This engagement  is expected
to improve  portfolio  performance  and strengthen  the City's  investment  program  going  forward  by
adding  layers  of compliance,  reporting,  credit  research,  and trading  capabilities  across all eligible
asset classes.

As of December  31, 2025,  the City's  General  Fund  had a positive  cash balance  of $18.4  million
(Attachment  B - Schedule  of Cash Balances  - December  31, 2025).

PURPOSE:  Each jurisdiction  in California  is required  to create an annual  progress  report  (APR)  on the
status  and progress  in implementing  the General  Plan  and Housing  Element  and submit  it to the State
Department  of Housing  and Cornrnunity  Development  (HCD)  by April  Ist of the following  calendar  year.
Additionally,  jurisdictions  must  also submit  the General  Plan  APR  to both  the Office  of Planning  and
Research  (OPR).  The attached  reports  have been compiled  in compliance  with  the State's  requirements.

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Receiving  and filing  the General  Plan and Housing  Element  APRs  for calendar  year 2025;
  and
  b.  Directing  staff to file the APRs  to HCD  and OPR prior  to the April  1, 2026,  deadline.

FISCAL  IMPACT:  None.

ALIGNMENT  WITH  COUNCIL  GOALS:  The filing  of the General  Plan and Housing  Element  APRs
supports  the goal  of creating  strong  and  sustainable  neighborhoods.  Monitoring  housing  development
ensures  the City  is making  progress  in the creation  of new housing  stock  and working  toward  creating
greater  housing  opportunities  for South  Gate residents.

ANALYSIS:  California  Government  Code  Section  65400  requires  local  governments  to prepare  and
provide  an annual  report  to the legislative  body  (Mayor  and City  Council)  on the stahis of its progress  in
implementing  the Housing  Element  of its General  Plan. These reports  are required  to be submitted  to the
HCD  each year for the reporting  period  of the previous  calendar  year by April  ls',  Failure  to submit  this
report  by the deadline  would  leave the City  in violation  of this State law.

BACKGROUND:  The General  Plan APR  is a surnrnary  of activities  affecting  the General  Plan during
the reporting  year. The Housing  Element  APR  is prepared  using  the standard  forms  developed  by HCD
and must be submitted  either  via online  portal  or email.

The Housing  Element  APR tracks  the City's  progress  in developing  residential  units  in the various  income

Element.

RHNA  Progress

The  City's  RHNA  is summarized  in Table  #1 below  by  income  level.  Income  levels  are set by the
Department  of Housing  and Community  Development  (HCD).  Each year HCD  publishes  annual  tables  of
official  federal  and State income  limits.  HCD's  limits  are based on surveys  of local  area median  income
(AMI).  The most current  survey  is based on information  released  on April  23, 2025,  which  set the AMI  in
Los Angeles  County  at $74,600  for a single-person  household.  It is adjusted  by the number  of persons  per
household.  Beginning  in  2022,  California  established  acutely  low-income  household  levels.  After
calculating  AMI  levels,  HCD  sets the maximum  acutely  low-income  limit  to equal  15 percent  of the
county's  AMI,  adjusted  for family  size. The income  categories  for a single-person  household  are as follows:

  Acutely  Low  15% or below  of AMI  Below  $11,200
  Extremely  low income  15% to 30% of AMI  Below  $31,850
  Very  low income  30% to 50% of AMI  Below  $53,000
  Low  income  50% to 80% of AMI  Below  $84,850
  Moderate  income  80% to 120%  of AMI  Below  $89,550

In Los Angeles  County,  as well  as several  other  counties  in the state, the very  low-income  limit  does not
equal 50% of AMI  (and the low-income  limit  does not equal 80% of AMI).  There  are many  exceptions  to
the arithmetic  calculation  of income  limits.  These  include  adjustments  for high  housing  cost relative  to
income,  the  application  of  state  nonmetropolitan  income  limits  in  low-income  areas,  and  national

 maximums  in high-income  areas. In Los Angeles  County,  as well  as several  others,  the magnitude  of these
adjustments  results  in the low-income  limit  exceeding  AMI.

The South Gate General Plan complies with LCI's General Plan Guidelines.  The following is a
summary of actions related to the General Plan and updated Municipal Code sections over the
past year:

  Moratoriums

  The City currently  has no moratoriums  related  to the General  Plan.

  Updates

  No other elements  or plans were amended  during this reporting  period.  The  last
  comprehensive  update to the General Plan occurred in 2009.

  On January 23, 2024, the City adopted the Final "Draft" 2021-2029  Housing Element
  Update to incorporate  comments received from the State Department  of Housing and
  Community  Development  (HCD). The Final "Draft" Housing Element was found by
  HCD to be in compliance  with State housing law.

  Zoninq  Code Amendment

  In December  2024, the Planning  Commission  recommended  to the City Council
  approval of an ordinance  amendment  to Chapter 11.21 (Land Use Types) of Title
  11 (Zoning) of the South Gate Municipal Code (SGMC), relating to restaurants  with
  ancillary  alcohol sales within the Open Space (OS) zoning district. However,  the
  recommendation  was not accepted  by City Council and the amendment  failed on
  February 25, 2025.

  On October 14, 2025, the City adopted  Ordinance  No. 2025-01-CC  updating its
  Accessory  Dwelling Unit (ADU) Ordinance  found in Title 11, Chapter 11.43 of the
  South Gate Municipal  Code (SGMC),  to align with State law and amend certain
  requirements.

  Specific  Plans:

  The City has adopted three specific plans: Recycle City Specific Plan; Hollydale Village
  Specific Plan; and Tweedy Boulevard  Specific Plan. Additional provisions were adopted
  for the southwestern  corner of Atlantic Avenue and Tweedy Boulevard, which is part of
  the Tweedy  Boulevard  Specific  Plan. Projects within these specific  plan areas are
  reviewed  based on specific  standards  and policies.  No changes  were made to the
  specific plans during this review period.

  In 2025, the City began the process of revisiting a plan for its Gateway District. The City
  began preparing the draft Gateway District Specific Plan (GDSP) in 2015; however, work

  Governments  (SCAG)  for a Regional  Early Action  Planning  (REAP)  Subregional
